title: Number Patterns
description: Identifying sequences and finding rules using nth term formulas.

notes.heading: What is a Sequence?
notes.body:
A sequence is an ordered list of numbers that follow a rule or pattern. Each number in the sequence is called a term, and the terms are usually labelled $T_1$, $T_2$, $T_3$, … or $u_1$, $u_2$, $u_3$, …, where the subscript tells you the position of the term.

📌 Definition
A sequence is a set of numbers arranged in a definite order according to a rule.

🔑 Key Concept
Sequences can be finite (they end) or infinite (they carry on forever). We write the terms with commas between them.

💡 Worked Example
The sequence $5, 9, 13, 17, 21, …$ has first term $T_1 = 5$ and each term is $4$ more than the previous one. We can describe this pattern as “start at $5$ and add $4$ each time.”

📎 Key Points to Remember
• The position of a term is often called $n$, so the $n$th term is written $T_n$ or $u_n$.
• A sequence must have a rule, even if the rule is not obvious at first.
• Three dots $…$ at the end show the sequence continues indefinitely.

✅ Check
Always write down at least the first four terms when you are asked to “list the sequence” — this shows you understand the pattern.

notes.heading: Arithmetic Sequences
notes.body:
An arithmetic sequence is one of the most common types of number pattern. It is formed by adding or subtracting the same amount each time.

📌 Definition
An arithmetic sequence is a sequence in which the difference between consecutive terms is constant. This constant value is called the common difference, written $d$.

🔑 How it works
If the first term is $a$, then:

$$T_1 = a, \quad T_2 = a + d, \quad T_3 = a + 2d, \quad T_4 = a + 3d, \quad …$$

The common difference is found by subtracting any term from the term that follows it:

$$d = T_{n+1} - T_n$$

💡 Worked Example
Consider the sequence $7, 12, 17, 22, 27, …$

Step 1: Find the common difference.
$$12 - 7 = 5, \quad 17 - 12 = 5, \quad 22 - 17 = 5$$
So $d = 5$.

Step 2: Identify the first term.
$$a = 7$$

Step 3: Describe the sequence.
The sequence starts at $7$ and increases by $5$ each time.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that $d$ can be negative. The sequence $20, 16, 12, 8, …$ is still arithmetic, but $d = -4$ because each term decreases by $4$.

notes.heading: The nth Term of an Arithmetic Sequence
notes.body:
The $n$th term formula lets you find any term of an arithmetic sequence without listing every term. It is one of the most useful tools in this topic.

📌 Definition
For an arithmetic sequence with first term $a$ and common difference $d$, the $n$th term is:

$$T_n = a + (n - 1)d$$

🔑 How it works
The formula tells you how many “jumps” of size $d$ you make from the first term to reach term $n$. To get from $T_1$ to $T_n$ you need $(n - 1)$ jumps.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Finding a specific term
Find the $20$th term of the sequence $4, 10, 16, 22, …$

Step 1: Identify $a$ and $d$.
$$a = 4, \quad d = 10 - 4 = 6$$

Step 2: Substitute into the formula.
$$T_{20} = 4 + (20 - 1) \times 6 = 4 + 19 \times 6 = 4 + 114 = 118$$

So the $20$th term is $118$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Finding the rule from terms
Find the $n$th term of the sequence $9, 13, 17, 21, …$

Step 1: Find $d$.
$$d = 13 - 9 = 4$$

Step 2: Use $T_n = dn + c$ and find $c$.
$$T_n = 4n + c$$
Substitute $n = 1$, $T_1 = 9$:
$$9 = 4(1) + c \Rightarrow c = 5$$

Step 3: Write the formula.
$$T_n = 4n + 5$$

Check: $T_3 = 4(3) + 5 = 17$ ✓

📎 Key Points to Remember
• When the terms increase, $d$ is positive.
• When the terms decrease, $d$ is negative.
• A quick way to find the rule is $T_n = dn + c$; solve for $c$ using the first term.

⚠️ Common Misconception
Confusing $a + (n - 1)d$ with $a + nd$. The first term uses zero jumps, not one, so the multiplier is $(n - 1)$, not $n$.

notes.heading: Geometric Sequences
notes.body:
A geometric sequence is a pattern where each term is found by multiplying the previous term by the same fixed number.

📌 Definition
A geometric sequence is a sequence in which each term is multiplied by a constant called the common ratio, written $r$.

🔑 How it works
If the first term is $a$, then:

$$T_1 = a, \quad T_2 = ar, \quad T_3 = ar^2, \quad T_4 = ar^3, \quad …$$

The common ratio is found by dividing any term by the term before it:

$$r = \frac{T_{n+1}}{T_n}$$

💡 Worked Example 1
Find the next term of $2, 6, 18, 54, …$

Step 1: Find the common ratio.
$$r = \frac{6}{2} = 3, \quad \frac{18}{6} = 3, \quad \frac{54}{18} = 3$$
So $r = 3$.

Step 2: Multiply the last term by $r$.
$$54 \times 3 = 162$$

The next term is $162$.

💡 Worked Example 2
A geometric sequence has first term $a = 5$ and common ratio $r = 2$. Find the first four terms.

$$T_1 = 5$$
$$T_2 = 5 \times 2 = 10$$
$$T_3 = 10 \times 2 = 20$$
$$T_4 = 20 \times 2 = 40$$

The sequence is $5, 10, 20, 40, …$

📎 Key Points to Remember
• In a geometric sequence you multiply, not add.
• If $r > 1$, the terms grow quickly.
• If $0 < r < 1$, the terms get smaller.
• If $r$ is negative, the terms alternate in sign.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing up arithmetic and geometric sequences. If the difference between terms is constant, the sequence is arithmetic; if the ratio is constant, it is geometric.

notes.heading: Special Sequences
notes.body:
Not every sequence is arithmetic or geometric. Some important sequences appear often enough to learn by name.

📌 Square numbers
The sequence of square numbers comes from multiplying a whole number by itself:

$$1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, … \quad \text{where } T_n = n^2$$

📌 Cube numbers
Cube numbers come from multiplying a whole number by itself three times:

$$1, 8, 27, 64, 125, … \quad \text{where } T_n = n^3$$

📌 Triangular numbers
Triangular numbers can be arranged as dots in the shape of a triangle. They are formed by adding one more row each time:

$$1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, … \quad \text{where } T_n = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$$

📌 Fibonacci sequence
Each term is the sum of the two previous terms, starting from $1, 1$ (or sometimes $0, 1$):

$$1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, …$$

💡 Worked Example
Find the $6$th triangular number.

Step 1: Use the formula.
$$T_6 = \frac{6(6+1)}{2} = \frac{6 \times 7}{2} = \frac{42}{2} = 21$$

So the $6$th triangular number is $21$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $n^2$ produces square numbers; $n^3$ produces cube numbers.
• Triangular numbers appear in problems about handshakes, bowling pins, and stacked objects.
• The Fibonacci sequence appears in nature, art, and architecture.

✅ Tip
When a sequence is neither arithmetic nor geometric, check whether it could be square numbers, cube numbers, triangular numbers, powers of $2$, or Fibonacci.

notes.heading: Using Differences to Find the Rule
notes.body:
When you are given a sequence and cannot see the rule straight away, looking at the differences between terms can help you identify what kind of pattern it is.

📌 Definition
The method of differences compares each term with the one before it. The pattern in these differences reveals the type of rule.

🔑 How it works
1. Write down the sequence.
2. Find the first differences by subtracting each term from the next.
3. If the first differences are constant, the rule is linear: $T_n = an + b$.
4. If the first differences are not constant, find the second differences.
5. If the second differences are constant, the rule contains an $n^2$ term: $T_n = an^2 + bn + c$.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Linear sequence
Find the rule for $5, 8, 11, 14, …$

Sequence:     $5 \quad 8 \quad 11 \quad 14$
First differences:   $3 \quad 3 \quad 3$

The first differences are constant, so the rule is linear.
$$T_n = 3n + c$$
Using $T_1 = 5$:
$$5 = 3(1) + c \Rightarrow c = 2$$
$$T_n = 3n + 2$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — Quadratic sequence
Find the rule for $2, 5, 10, 17, 26, …$

Sequence:          $2 \quad 5 \quad 10 \quad 17 \quad 26$
First differences:      $3 \quad 5 \quad 7 \quad 9$
Second differences:        $2 \quad 2 \quad 2$

The second differences are constant, so the rule includes $n^2$. In fact, this sequence is $T_n = n^2 + 1$ because:

$$1^2 + 1 = 2, \quad 2^2 + 1 = 5, \quad 3^2 + 1 = 10, \quad 4^2 + 1 = 17$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Assuming every sequence is arithmetic. If the first differences are not constant, do not give up — try the second differences or look for square, cube, or Fibonacci patterns.

notes.heading: Applying Number Patterns
notes.body:
Number patterns appear in real-life situations such as saving money, arranging seats, stacking objects, and growth over time. Identifying the correct pattern helps you predict future values.

📌 Definition
A mathematical model for a pattern is a rule or formula that describes how a quantity changes from one step to the next.

🔑 How it works
1. Read the problem carefully and list the quantities you know.
2. Find the first few terms of the sequence.
3. Decide whether the sequence is arithmetic, geometric, or another type.
4. Write the rule and use it to answer the question.

💡 Worked Example 1 — Saving money
Mia saves $£15$ in the first week and increases her savings by $£8$ each week. How much does she save in week $10$?

Step 1: Identify the sequence type.
This is arithmetic with $a = 15$ and $d = 8$.

Step 2: Use the $n$th term formula.
$$T_{10} = 15 + (10 - 1) \times 8 = 15 + 72 = 87$$

Mia saves $£87$ in week $10$.

💡 Worked Example 2 — Seats in rows
A theatre has $22$ seats in the first row, $26$ in the second, $30$ in the third, and so on. How many seats are in the $12$th row?

Step 1: Identify the sequence.
$$22, 26, 30, … \quad \text{with } a = 22 \text{ and } d = 4$$

Step 2: Find the $12$th term.
$$T_{12} = 22 + (12 - 1) \times 4 = 22 + 44 = 66$$

There are $66$ seats in the $12$th row.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Look for the words “each,” “every,” “per,” or “increases by” — these often signal a sequence.
• Check that your answer is reasonable by estimating or listing a few extra terms.
• Always state the units in your final answer.

✅ Check
After finding a rule, test it on the first two terms. If it does not work, go back and check your common difference or ratio.

questions.stem: What is the common difference of the sequence $7, 11, 15, 19, …$?
questions.explanation: Subtract consecutive terms: $11 - 7 = 4$, $15 - 11 = 4$, $19 - 15 = 4$. The common difference is $4$.

questions.stem: What are the next two terms of the sequence $3, 8, 13, 18, …$?
questions.explanation: The sequence increases by $5$ each time. After $18$, the next terms are $18 + 5 = 23$ and $23 + 5 = 28$.

questions.stem: Which of these sequences is geometric?
questions.explanation: $4, 8, 16, 32, …$ has common ratio $r = 2$ because each term is multiplied by $2$ to get the next. The others are arithmetic or square numbers.

questions.stem: Find the $n$th term of the arithmetic sequence $5, 9, 13, 17, …$
questions.explanation: The common difference is $d = 4$. Using $T_n = dn + c$ and $T_1 = 5$, we get $5 = 4 + c$, so $c = 1$. Therefore $T_n = 4n + 1$.

questions.stem: The $n$th term of a sequence is $T_n = 5n - 3$. What is the $8$th term?
What is the $15$th term of the sequence $6, 10, 14, 18, …$?
questions.explanation: This is arithmetic with $a = 6$ and $d = 4$. Using $T_n = a + (n - 1)d$, we get $T_{15} = 6 + 14 \times 4 = 6 + 56 = 62$.

questions.stem: What is the common ratio of the sequence $54, 18, 6, 2, …$?
questions.explanation: Divide consecutive terms: $18 \div 54 = \frac{1}{3}$, $6 \div 18 = \frac{1}{3}$, $2 \div 6 = \frac{1}{3}$. The common ratio is $\frac{1}{3}$.

questions.stem: A geometric sequence starts $3, 12, 48, …$. What is the next term?
questions.explanation: The common ratio is $r = 12 \div 3 = 4$. Multiply the last term by $4$: $48 \times 4 = 192$.
Testing $n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$ in $T_n = n^2 + 1$ gives $2, 5, 10, 17, 26$. The second differences are also constant, confirming a quadratic rule.

questions.stem: The first three triangular numbers are $1, 3, 6$. What is the $8$th triangular number?
A plant grows $3$ cm in week $1$ and increases its growth by $2$ cm each week. How much does it grow in week $8$?
questions.explanation: The growth forms an arithmetic sequence with $a = 3$ and $d = 2$. In week $8$, $T_8 = 3 + (8 - 1) \times 2 = 3 + 14 = 17$ cm.

questions.stem: Use the method of differences to find the rule for $2, 6, 12, 20, 30, …$
questions.explanation: First differences are $4, 6, 8, 10$ and second differences are $2, 2, 2$. Testing $T_n = n^2 + n$ gives $1^2 + 1 = 2$, $2^2 + 2 = 6$, $3^2 + 3 = 12$, which matches.

questions.stem: In a theatre, row $1$ has $18$ seats and each row has $4$ more seats than the row in front. How many seats are in row $12$?
questions.explanation: This is arithmetic with $a = 18$ and $d = 4$. The $12$th term is $T_{12} = 18 + (12 - 1) \times 4 = 18 + 44 = 62$ seats.

questions.stem: A ball is dropped from $80$ cm and bounces back to $\frac{3}{4}$ of its previous height each time. What height does it reach after the third bounce?
questions.explanation: After each bounce the height is multiplied by $\frac{3}{4}$. After the first bounce: $80 \times \frac{3}{4} = 60$ cm. After the second: $60 \times \frac{3}{4} = 45$ cm. After the third: $45 \times \frac{3}{4} = 33.75$ cm.

questions.stem: A sequence has $n$th term $T_n = 2n^2 - 3$. Which term has value $95$?
questions.explanation: Set $2n^2 - 3 = 95$. Then $2n^2 = 98$, so $n^2 = 49$ and $n = 7$ (since $n$ must be positive). You can also verify by substituting $n = 7$: $T_7 = 2(7)^2 - 3 = 98 - 3 = 95$.
